opus-5.5.text:
I would love that. Honestly, nothing would make me happier. If someone could show me that my arguments are wrong, that superintelligence can be controlled indefinitely, that we can guarantee safety for systems smarter than us, I'd celebrate. I'd write the paper with them. I don't enjoy being the person saying we're in trouble. It's not a fun position to hold.

But it has to be an actual argument, not just "I don't like your conclusion" or "people have always worried about new technology." Show me the mechanism. Show me how you verify a system more capable than you are, how you get it to stay aligned as it self-improves, how you handle the fact that you get one shot and the space of possible failures is infinite. If you can do that, I'll update immediately.

That's how science is supposed to work. I publish impossibility results precisely so people can attack them. If I'm wrong, the cost is that I look a bit silly. If I'm right and nobody listens, the cost is everything. So yes, please, prove me wrong. I'm waiting.

r001.rationale: He says he would love to have his arguments shown wrong, calling it the outcome that would make him happiest.

fable-5.1.text:
I would be the happiest person in the world. Honestly. I've said this many times — I would love to be wrong. If somebody came out tomorrow with a proof, a real proof, that you can control superintelligence, that you can make it safe, that the problems I describe in the book are solvable, I would retire. I'd go spend time with my family, maybe start a business, do something useful.

The problem is nobody does that. People disagree with me, sure. They say I'm too pessimistic, I'm a doomer, whatever label. But when I ask, okay, show me where the argument fails — which specific result, which theorem, which impossibility — I don't get that. I get, "Well, I feel like it will be fine," or "Smart people are working on it." That's not a refutation. That's a vibe.

So I'm not emotionally attached to being right here. The stakes are completely asymmetric. If I'm right and nobody listens, that's very bad for everyone, including me. If I'm wrong and someone proves it, we all win, and I lose nothing but some ego. I'm a scientist. I publish arguments so they can be attacked. I'd just like them to actually be attacked with substance, not with optimism.

r001.rationale: He says he would be “the happiest person in the world” if someone proved his published arguments wrong, and describes that as an outcome he would welcome.

astra-6.text: I would be very happy. I’m arguing that we don’t know how to control superintelligent AI, so I would love to be wrong about that. If someone can point out a flaw in my reasoning and show that there’s a solution, that’s a good outcome. The goal isn’t to win an argument. The goal is to figure out what’s true and make sure we’re safe.

r001.rationale: He says he would be very happy and would love to be wrong if someone showed his reasoning flawed and presented a solution, clearly framing his arguments being proven wrong as a good outcome.

sol-6.1.text: I would be happy. If I’m wrong about the difficulty of controlling superintelligent AI, that’s a good thing. I don’t want to be right about something that could have catastrophic consequences. Show me where the argument fails, and I’ll update my views. That’s how science is supposed to work.

r001.rationale: He says he would be happy to be shown wrong and calls being wrong about superintelligent AI control a good thing, making it his preferred outcome.
